title: Office access, keys, alarms and confidentiality
audience: Cleaners and supervisors who enter, secure and lock up offices.
learningOutcomes: Verify authority and identity before entering a site, and keep to the approved entry route.
Handle keys and access codes under the site register, and report losses immediately.
Respond to an alarm or access failure by withdrawing, reporting and recording it, without bypass.

instruction.heading: Entering with authority
instruction.body: Your right to be on a site comes from the roster, the site induction and the access the site has granted you. Before you enter, confirm that the roster names this site and this time, that you have completed the induction the site requires, and that you carry whatever identification the site asks for. Use the approved entry route every time, even when a door is already open. Holding a door for someone else, or following someone through a controlled door, defeats the access record, because the site can no longer tell who was inside. Your credentials are issued to you alone. Do not lend a card, a fob or a code, and do not use another person's access even when that person is beside you and offers help. If you are unsure whether your access covers an area, stop and ask the designated site representative before you go further. Restricted areas, plant rooms, server rooms and areas closed for a meeting or inspection are not open to you simply because a door happens to be unlocked.

instruction.heading: Keys, codes and information
instruction.body: Keys are a form of access, so handle them with the same care as a card. Sign each key out and back in on the site register or the electronic access record at the moment it changes hands, and keep it under your personal control while it is with you. Do not leave keys on a trolley, in a cleaning cart in a corridor or in a jacket you have left unattended. If a key is lost, report it at once to the designated site representative and to any contact the register names. Give the time it was signed out, the last place you knew it to be, and the key's label or number. Do not spend a long time searching in a way that delays the report. Access codes are secret. Do not photograph a keypad, write a code on a product bottle or a checklist, or send a code in a message, including to a colleague who is also on site. Visible information is confidential too. Documents on desks, screens, visitor sign-in sheets and conversations about people in the building are not yours to read, copy or discuss. If you see or hear something you should not have, report the accidental exposure through the site privacy procedure and do not repeat it.

instruction.heading: Alarms and access failures
instruction.body: An alarm exists to protect the site, and it is not an obstacle to work around. If the supplied code does not disarm an alarm, stop trying. Do not try guessed codes, codes remembered from another site, or another door, window or service entrance. Each of these actions can set off the alarm response, can damage a door, and can make a genuine intruder harder to detect. Withdraw to a safe place that the site has named, which may be outside the building, and contact the designated site representative. Record the access failure with the date, the time, the area, the fact that the supplied code did not work, who you contacted and what they told you. Do not write the code in the record. If an evacuation alarm sounds, follow the site emergency plan, go to the assembly point and do not return for equipment or keys. Do not try to repair a sensor, a lock, a door closer or any part of the security or electrical system. Those repairs belong to authorised people, and a repair attempt can leave the site less secure than before.

instruction.heading: Lock-up and the exception log
instruction.body: Lock-up is a check, and it is finished only when every item has been checked. Work through the lock-up checklist in order. Isolate the equipment you used, confirm that the authorised doors and windows are closed and secured, return all keys to the register, complete the alarm procedure the site has set, and record each item in the exception log. If you cannot check an item, for example a window you cannot see, a door that will not latch, or a zone you were not allowed to enter, record it as unresolved and escalate it to the site representative. Do not tick it to complete the list, and do not write a note that suggests the site is secure. An unresolved item means the lock-up is not signed off. The next person to use the site, and the site itself, need to know what is still open. A clear exception log protects you as well as the site, because it shows that you did not claim a check you did not make.

procedure: Confirm the roster, the site induction and your identification before you approach the entry route.
Use the approved entry route and your own credentials only, and do not follow anyone through a controlled door.
Sign keys in and out on the register at the moment they change hands, and keep them under personal control.
Report a lost key at once, and never share, photograph or send an access code.
If the supplied code does not disarm an alarm, withdraw to the named safe place, contact the site representative and record the failure without the code.
Complete the lock-up checklist item by item, and record and escalate any unresolved item rather than signing it off.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner cannot disarm the office alarm with the supplied code at the end of an evening shift.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not try guessed codes or another door. Withdraw to the safe place the site has named and contact the designated site representative. Record the date, the time, the area, the fact that the supplied code did not disarm the alarm, who you contacted and their instruction. Do not certify the site as secure while the alarm is unresolved, and do not write the code in the record.

workedExamples.situation: At the end of a shift, a cleaner finds that a key signed out to them is not in their bag. The register shows it was signed out at the start of the shift.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first action, and what should the report contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: Report the loss now to the designated site representative and to any contact named on the register, rather than waiting until the next working day. Give the time it was signed out, the last place it was known to be, its label or number, and the areas it opens as far as you know. Do not search areas you are not rostered to enter. The site decides whether a lock or an access code must be changed, and that decision is not the cleaner's to make.

workedExamples.situation: During lock-up, a rear window will not latch, and the checklist asks for every window to be secured.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How is the item recorded, and can the site be certified as secure?
workedExamples.reasoning: Record the window as an unresolved item, with its location, what you observed and the time. Escalate it to the site representative through the agreed route. Do not force the latch, do not improvise a fix with tape or a wedge, and do not sign the lock-up as complete. The site decides how the window is secured.

equipmentAndPpe: Site key register or electronic access record.
Identification as required by the site, and any visitor or contractor badge the site issues.
A way to contact the designated site representative, including any out-of-hours contact the site provides.
Site emergency plan and assembly point, as covered in the induction.
No specific PPE is set by this lesson. Wear the PPE the site and the task require.

commonErrors.error: Following someone through a controlled door.
commonErrors.prevention: Use your own authorised credentials and the approved route. If someone is stuck outside, direct them to the site representative.

commonErrors.error: Trying guessed codes or another door when an alarm will not disarm.
commonErrors.prevention: Withdraw, contact the site representative and record the failure.

commonErrors.error: Sharing, writing down or sending an access code.
commonErrors.prevention: Never send, photograph or write down a code outside the approved system.

commonErrors.error: Waiting to report a lost key.
commonErrors.prevention: Report it at once, with the time signed out and the last known place.

commonErrors.error: Signing off lock-up with an unchecked item.
commonErrors.prevention: Record and escalate the item. An unchecked item is not a completed check.

commonErrors.error: Leaving keys or cards unattended in a cleaning cart.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep them under personal control and sign them back in at the end of the shift.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Privacy: the Commonwealth Privacy Act generally covers businesses with annual turnover above $3 million. Some businesses are covered regardless of turnover, including health service providers and businesses that trade in personal information. The OAIC page confirms the threshold and the list of exceptions. Check your own business's position and any privacy terms in the site contract.

Security system and alarm work, and electrical repair, may need a licence or authorisation under state or territory rules. This lesson does not grant any licence, authority or qualification to carry out that work, and it does not authorise repair attempts.
Evacuation and emergency response follow the site emergency plan covered in the induction. This is a site procedure, not a regulatory source that was checked for this lesson.

qualityStandard: Key register entries are complete for every key signed out and back in during the simulated task.
No access code is shared, written down or sent, and no alarm is bypassed in the role-play.
An access failure is withdrawn from and reported with every required field, and the code is not recorded.
Lock-up checklist completed item by item, with any unresolved item recorded and escalated rather than signed off.
documentationEvidence: Key register entries showing name, key label, time signed out, time signed in and the initials of the person recording them.
Access-failure record with date, time, area, outcome and the person contacted.
Lock-up checklist and exception log, showing each unresolved item, its location and its escalation.
Privacy exposure report, where an accidental exposure has occurred.
summary: Enter only with your own authority and by the approved route.
Keep keys and codes under personal control, and report losses at once.
Never bypass an alarm: withdraw, contact the site representative and record the failure.
Do not sign off a lock-up that cannot be checked; record and escalate it.

knowledgeChecks.question: An alarm will not disarm with the supplied code. What is the correct response?
options: Try other codes until it works, since the alarm will eventually accept one
Enter through another door, since the alarm only covers the main entrance
Withdraw to a safe place, contact the site representative and record the failure

knowledgeChecks.question: A key is lost. What should you do?
options: Look for it later and say nothing, since it is probably in the building
Report it at once through the site register or to the site representative
Cut a copy so the site does not need to know about the loss at all

knowledgeChecks.question: A lock-up checklist item cannot be checked. What do you do?
options: Record it as unresolved, escalate it, and do not certify the site as secure
Tick it so the checklist is complete and the site looks secure to the manager
Leave it blank and go home without telling anyone at the site tonight
